# THREAD A — BUS FACTOR / TRUCK FACTOR

## A1. The canonical academic paper: Avelino, Passos, Hora, Valente (ICPC 2016)

**"A Novel Approach for Estimating Truck Factors"**, Guilherme Avelino, Leonardo Passos, Andre Hora, Marco Tulio Valente, *24th IEEE International Conference on Program Comprehension (ICPC 2016)*, pp. 1–10. Preprint: arXiv:1604.06766 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.06766 (PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1604.06766). Tool: https://github.com/aserg-ufmg/Truck-Factor

**Definition (verbatim):**
> "A system's truck factor (TF) is defined as 'the number of people on your team that have to be hit by a truck (or quit) before the project is in serious trouble'."

> "Truck Factor (TF) is a metric proposed by the agile community as a tool to identify concentration of knowledge in software development environments. It states the minimal number of developers that have to be hit by a truck (or quit) before a project is incapacitated. In other words, TF helps to measure how prepared is a project to deal with developer turnover."

> "Systems with a low truck factor spot strong dependencies towards specific personnel, forming knowledge silos among developer teams."

**Their definition of authorship (important nuance — it's not "who created the file"):**
> "Authorship, in this case, is not a strict notion. Stated otherwise, authorship is not a matter of who creates a file. Rather, authorship is a statement of who will be able to maintain a file from the latest system snapshot onward."

**The DOA formula, verbatim from the paper:**
> "DOA(md, fp) = 3.293 + 1.098 × FA(md, fp) + 0.164 × DL(md, fp) − 0.321 × ln(1 + AC(md, fp))"

> "From the equation, DOA depends on three factors: (i) first authorship (FA): if md originally created f, FA is 1; otherwise it is 0; (ii) number of deliveries (DL): number of changes in f made by md; and (iii) number of acceptances (AC): number of changes in f made by any developer, except md."

> "DOA weights contributions differently, accounting for both changes of a developer in a file (increases DOA), as well as the changes performed by others (decreases DOA)."

**The "main developer" thresholds, verbatim:**
> "A normalized DOA-value ranges from 0 to 1. We grant 1 to the developer with the highest absolute DOA among all developers that worked on f; altogether, we consider a developer as an author of a file if its resulting normalized DOA is greater than a threshold k and its absolute DOA is not lower than a value m. Currently, k and m stands as configurable parameters in our approach. As we show in Section IV-B, k = 0.75 and m = 3.293 seem to provide good results."

So: **normalized DOA ≥ 0.75 × max DOA for that file, AND absolute DOA ≥ 3.293** — 3.293 being exactly the intercept of Fritz's regression, i.e. the DOA of someone who has done nothing.

**The 50% coverage threshold, verbatim:**
> "Our estimation relies on a coverage assumption: a system will face serious delays or will be likely discontinued if its current set of authors covers less than 50% of the current set of files in the system."

The algorithm (Algorithm 1 in the paper) is a greedy heuristic: `while A ≠ ∅ { coverage ← getCoverage(F, A); if coverage < 0.5 break; A ← removeTopAuthor(A); tf ← tf + 1 }`.

**Headline empirical findings (exact numbers, verbatim):**
> "we propose a novel (and automated) approach for estimating TF-values, which we execute against a corpus of 133 popular project in GitHub… Among others, we find that the majority of our target systems (65%) have TF ≤ 2."

> "Figure 5 presents the distribution of the truck factor amongst our subjects. The first, second, and third quartiles are 1, 2, and 4, respectively. Most systems have a small truck factor: 45 systems (34%) have TF = 1 (e.g., mbostock/d3 and less/less.js); in 42 systems (31%), TF = 2 including well-known systems such as clojure/clojure, cucumber/cucumber, ashkenas/backbone and elasticsearch/elasticsearch."

> "torvalds/linux has TF = 57, followed by fzaninotto/Faker (TF = 23) and android/platform frameworks base (TF = 19). Other well-known systems include php/php-src (TF = 18), git/git (TF = 12), v8/v8 (TF = 11), and rails/rails (TF = 9)."

Corpus scale: *"133 systems in GitHub. In total, such systems have over 373K files and 41 MLOC; their combined evolution history sums to over 2 million commits."*

**Validation:** *"in 84% of valid answers developers agree or partially agree that the TF's authors are the main authors of their systems; in 53% we receive a positive or partially positive answer regarding our estimated truck factors."* (106 respondents, 84 of them top-10 contributors, 62 systems.)

**Author-ratio findings (relevant to "concentration is normal"):**
> "the first, second, and third quartiles are 16%, 23%, and 36%" (proportion of developers who qualify as authors). And: *"Backbone is also an example, with only six authors amongst its 248 developers. These six authors monopolize 67% of commits."*

**On mitigation, verbatim:** *"According to the surveyed developers, documentation is the most effective development practice to overcome a truck factor event, followed by the existence of an active community…"*

## A2. The DOA formula's origin: Fritz et al. (ICSE 2010)

**"A Degree-of-Knowledge Model to Capture Source Code Familiarity"**, Thomas Fritz, Jingwen Ou, Gail C. Murphy, Emerson Murphy-Hill, *ICSE 2010*, pp. 385–394. PDF: https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~fritz/papers/icse10_dok_web.pdf

I verified the coefficients directly against Table 1 of the paper. **They are exactly right, and they come from a multiple linear regression on developer self-ratings:**

| | Weighting | Std. Error | p-value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intercept | 3.293 | 0.133 | <0.001 |
| FA | 1.098 | 0.179 | <0.001 |
| DL | 0.164 | 0.053 | 0.002 |
| ln(1 + AC) | −0.321 | 0.105 | 0.002 |
| ln(1 + DOI) | 0.190 | 0.100 | 0.059 |

The **full DOK** equation, verbatim:
> "DOK = 3.293 + 1.098 ∗ FA + 0.164 ∗ DL − 0.321 ∗ ln(1 + AC) + 0.19 ∗ ln(1 + DOI)"

The truck-factor literature uses only the first four terms (DOA) — the DOI term needs IDE interaction logs, which VCS mining doesn't have.

**Crucial caveat that almost nobody quoting this formula mentions, verbatim from Fritz et al.:**
> "The overall model has an estimated 'goodness of fit', R Square, of 0.25 (adjusted R Square is 0.23)… The correlation coefficient R that represents a measure of the overall fit between our predictor variables and the user rating is 0.50. The standard error of the estimate is 1.17. The 0.25 R Square value shows that our model does not predict the user rating completely."

Also: the model was fit on **246 ratings from seven developers** at one site, validated on 80 elements from two developers at a second site (Spearman rs = 0.3847, p = 0.0004). And: *"Determining weightings that might apply across a broader range of development situations would require gathering data from many more projects, which was not warranted at this early stage of investigation."* Those magic constants are far more contingent than their four-decimal precision suggests.

## A3. Cosentino, Cánovas Izquierdo, Cabot (SANER 2015)

**"Assessing the bus factor of Git repositories"**, Valerio Cosentino, Javier Luis Cánovas Izquierdo, Jordi Cabot, *2015 IEEE 22nd International Conference on Software Analysis, Evolution, and Reengineering (SANER)*, pp. 499–503. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1109/SANER.2015.7081864 · https://dblp.org/pers/hd/c/Cosentino:Valerio

The published PDF is paywalled (IEEE) and the HAL/ResearchGate/Academia mirrors all returned 403 to me, so I could not verify quotes against the original. **The canonical definition, quoted verbatim from a secondary source that quotes it in quotation marks** — Aliza Lisan and Boyana Norris, "Guiding Effort Allocation in Open-Source Software Projects Using Bus Factor Analysis," arXiv:2401.03303 (2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03303:
> "Formally known as the Bus Factor (BF) of a project and defined as 'the number of key developers who would need to be incapacitated to make a project unable to proceed'."

**The Cosentino algorithm described verbatim** in Jabrayilzade et al. (ICSE-SEIP 2022, §2.2, see A4):
> "Cosentino et al. [10] suggest a set of algorithms to compute the bus factor. The authors define the notion of primary and secondary developers. The file is abandoned when none of the primary or secondary developers who worked on it are present in the project. The bus factor problem happens when a certain amount of files is abandoned. The analysis can be carried out at either file-level or line-level of granularity. The authors suggest four different metrics (M1 to M4) for measuring contribution."
> "• M1 assigns all knowledge to the last contributor.
> • M2 considers every change with equal weight (e.g., if A committed to a file twice and B committed once, A has 2/3 knowledge and B has 1/3).
> • M3 is the same as M2, but consecutive changes are considered to be one change…
> • M4 adds weights to the changes; for a file with N commits, the oldest commit has weight 1, the second-oldest has weight 2, and so on."
> "For a file that has been edited by N contributors, primary developers are those who have done at least 100/N % of edits and secondary developers have done 100/N % > x > 50/N % of edits."

Same source, on the earlier **Zazworka/Ricca** approach and why it's weak:
> "The algorithm finds the minimal set of the developers such that these developers belong to more than X% of the project files… The threshold was varied from 50% to 70%." Findings: *"The threshold value affects the computed bus factor. • The idea that every person who did at least one commit to a file has knowledge about a file may be too strong. • There are 'update' commits that cover many files but probably do not signify that the committer has knowledge about them. • The algorithm performs well for the small projects, but seems to be problematic for projects with > 30 committers."*

## A4. Follow-up: abandonment and survival (ESEM 2019)

**"On the abandonment and survival of open source projects: An empirical investigation"**, Guilherme Avelino, Eleni Constantinou, Marco Tulio Valente, Alexander Serebrenik, *ESEM 2019*. arXiv:1906.08058 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.08058

> "We carefully select 1,932 popular GitHub projects and recover the abandoned and surviving projects… We found that 315 projects (16%) were abandoned and 128 of these projects (41%) survived because of new core developers who assumed the project development."

**The single most quotable stat in this whole thread, verbatim (boxed finding in the paper):**
> "Most open source projects have low TFs. In a sample of 1,932 projects, 57% have TF = 1 and 25% have TF = 2. The highest TF in our sample is 26 developers."

Note this is *higher concentration* than the 2016 paper (57%+25% = 82% at TF ≤ 2 vs. 65%), because the 2019 sample is broader, not only the very top projects.

> "It is possible to recover from TFDDs: 41% of the projects survived their last observed TFDD, usually by attracting a single new truck factor developer." And: *"Most of the projects faced only one TFDD situation (88%)."*

Motivating example, verbatim: *"OpenSSL, a cryptography library used by two-thirds of all Web servers, was maintained by a single developer until 2014, when a major bug, nicknamed Heartbleed, affecting millions of sites was detected in its implementation."*

## A5. 2020–2026 work: JetBrains Research

**"Bus Factor In Practice"**, Elgun Jabrayilzade (Bilkent), Mikhail Evtikhiev (JetBrains Research), Eray Tüzün (Bilkent), Vladimir Kovalenko (JetBrains Research), *ICSE-SEIP 2022*, pp. 97–106. arXiv:2202.01523 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.01523 · DOI https://doi.org/10.1145/3510457.3513082

> "Bus factor is a metric that identifies how resilient is the project to the sudden engineer turnover. It states the minimal number of engineers that have to be hit by a bus for a project to be stalled."

> "the existing tools for bus factor estimation focus solely on the data from version control systems, even though there exists other channels for knowledge generation and distribution. With a survey of 269 engineers, we find that the bus factor is perceived as an important problem in collective development…"

**Survey numbers, verbatim:**
> "51% of the survey participants know, what bus factor is, but only 19% of the respondents have ever worked on a project, where the bus factor was communicated to them. The bus factor of a project is perceived to be an important metric of project health: on a scale from one to five, 75% of the respondents rated its importance at 3 or higher, and 39% of the respondents have rated the importance at 4 or higher… 63% of the respondents over the course of past year have worked at least on one project, for which they felt there was a high risk of the bus factor reaching zero."

> "Respondents perceive the bus factor as the most important collective development problem out of seven problems that were suggested in the survey."

**Knowledge decay (directly relevant to any implementation):**
> "76% respondents believe that the knowledge decays with time, but there was little agreement for a typical time scale in which the knowledge about a particular file halves… Reported median halving time was 4 months. Most respondents believe that less than 20% of the files can be abandoned before project gets into trouble."

Note the tension: practitioners' intuition is ~20% file abandonment = trouble; Avelino's algorithm hardcodes 50%.

**Granularity disagreement:** *"39% of the respondents prefer project-level calculations, 16% prefer module-level calculations and 40% prefer team-level computations."*

**They restate Avelino's threshold rule formally:** *"An engineer e is an author of a file f if DOA(e, f) > 3.293 and DOA(e, f) > 0.75 ∗ max_e DOA(e, f)."*

**Their multimodal DOA replaces the Fritz coefficients wholesale**, adding code-review and meeting terms: `DOA_i = 3·FA + Σ_j(½ DL_i^j + RV_i^j + min(1, Σ_l MT_i^{l,j}/MT_E)) + 2.4 log(1 + ΣΣ DL_k^j) + 1.2 log(1 + ΣΣ RV_k^j) − …` — and it only beat the Avelino baseline marginally: *"We got slightly better MAE than the baseline (5.46 and 5.80)"*, F1 = 0.48 (P: 0.64, R: 0.39) on key-developer identification. **Also a damning practical finding: "We found that for two projects it predicted a key developer who is not active anymore (the last commit date was more than 1.5 years ago."** (i.e. no decay term in the baseline.)

**"Bus Factor Explorer"**, Egor Klimov, Muhammad Umair Ahmed, Nikolai Sviridov, Pouria Derakhshanfar, Eray Tüzün, Vladimir Kovalenko, *ICSE 2024 demo track*. arXiv:2403.08038 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.08038 · Tool: https://github.com/JetBrains-Research/bus-factor-explorer

> "Bus factor (BF) is a metric that tracks knowledge distribution in a project. It is the minimal number of engineers that have to leave for a project to stall."

**Their generic description of the whole algorithm family — the cleanest one-paragraph summary of the method in the literature:**
> "In most cases, the estimation consists of several steps. First, the algorithm mines VCS history to assess the amount of knowledge each engineer has for each file. Then, for each file, the algorithm produces a list of engineers who are experts in it, so that the departure of all engineers from the list leads to abandonment of the file. Finally, the algorithm produces the smallest set of engineers such that if all of them leave the project, more than a certain share of the files will be abandoned. The size of this set is considered the BF of the project."

> "Our tool allows users to identify the files and subsystems at risk of stalling in the event of developer turnover by analyzing the VCS history." Evaluated on **935 popular GitHub repositories**; *"our tool can analyze 12,000 commits in 25 seconds."*

Also relevant, and it explicitly bridges into Thread B: **"BFSig: Leveraging File Significance in Bus Factor Estimation"**, *ESEC/FSE 2023*, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3611643.3613877 (I hit a 403 and could not verify quotes — flagging it as a lead, not a source). The premise is exactly your Thread B: not all abandoned files are equally bad.

**Tornhill's own crucial qualifier** (docs, Knowledge Distribution — https://docs.enterprise.codescene.io/versions/4.4.27/guides/social/knowledge-distribution.html) — concentration is only a *risk multiplier*, not a risk by itself:
> "A knowledge island is code written mostly by one developer, but the code is of acceptable code health. You might still face a key personnel risk, but on-boarding new personnel in this area should be lower risk than in complex hotspots."

**This is the single most important framing point for your work: CodeScene does not treat "one author" as a risk. It treats "one author × hotspot × poor code health" as the risk.** Concentration is conditioned on blast radius — which is exactly the Thread A/Thread B join.

## A7. The normative question: is concentration bad and spreading good?

**Arguments that concentration is bad:**

*Software Engineering at Google* (Titus Winters, Tom Manshreck, Hyrum Wright, O'Reilly 2020), Ch. 3 "Knowledge Sharing" — https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch03.html
> Single Point of Failure: "A bottleneck that occurs when critical information is available from only a single person."
> On how it happens: "it can be easy to fall into a habit of 'Let me take care of that for you.'"
> On the resulting shape of expertise: a split "between people who know 'everything' and novices, with little middle ground."
> On information islands: "knowledge fragmentation that occurs in different parts of an organization that don't communicate with one another."

Martin Fowler, "CodeOwnership," martinfowler.com — https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CodeOwnership.html
> "Of the three the one I really don't like is strong code ownership."
> Strong: "Developers are only allowed to make changes to modules they own. If they need a change made to someone else's module they need to talk to the module owner and get them to make the change."
> Collective: "The code base is owned by the entire team and anyone may make changes anywhere."
> "Personally I prefer the dynamics of a collective code ownership team—particularly in the context of Extreme Programming."

Avelino et al. (ICPC 2016): *"If such knowledgeable personnel abandon the project, the system's lifecycle is seriously compromised, leading to delays in launching new releases, and ultimately to the discontinuation of the project as whole."* And the Python 1994 anecdote quoted in the paper: *"I just returned from a meeting in which the major objection to using Python was its dependence on Guido. They wanted to know if Python would survive if Guido disappeared."*

**The strongest evidence-backed argument that deep ownership is GOOD:**

**"Don't Touch My Code! Examining the Effects of Ownership on Software Quality"**, Christian Bird, Nachiappan Nagappan, Brendan Murphy, Harald Gall, Premkumar Devanbu, *ESEC/FSE 2011*, Szeged. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/dont-touch-my-code-examining-the-effects-of-ownership-on-software-quality/ · PDF: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/bird2011dtm.pdf

Definitions, verbatim:
> "Minor Contributor – A developer who has made changes to a component, but whose ownership is below 5% is considered a minor contributor to that component."
> "Major Contributor – A developer who has made changes to a component and whose ownership is at or above 5% is a major contributor to the component."
> "Ownership – proportion of ownership for the contributor with the highest proportion of ownership"

Their theory, verbatim — **note this is precisely the pro-concentration argument:**
> "If Ownership is high, that indicates that there is one developer who 'owns' the component and has a high level of expertise. This person can also act as a single point of contact for others who need to use the component, need changes to it, or just have questions about it. We theorize that when such a person exists, the software quality is higher resulting in fewer failures."
> "Hypothesis 2 - Software components with a high level of ownership will have fewer failures than components with lower top ownership levels."
> "Hypothesis 1 - Software components with many minor contributors will have more failures than software components that have fewer."

Findings, verbatim:
> "1. The number of minor contributors has a strong positive relationship with both pre- and post-release failures even when controlling for metrics such as size, churn, and complexity."
> "2. Higher levels of ownership for the top contributor to a component results in fewer failures when controlling for the same metrics, but the effect is smaller than the number of minor contributors."
> "We found that high levels of ownership, specifically operationalized as high values of Ownership and Major, and low values of Minor, are associated with less defects."

Their recommendations, verbatim — **these are anti-spreading:**
> "1. Changes made by minor contributors should be reviewed with more scrutiny… When possible, major contributors should perform these code inspections."
> "2. Potential minor contributors should communicate desired changes to developers experienced with the respective binary… Rather than making a desired change directly, these developers should contact a major contributor and communicate the desired change so that it can be made by someone who has higher levels of expertise."
> "3. Components with low ownership should be given priority by QA resources."

And their own scope caveat, verbatim:
> "Microsoft employs strong ownership practices and our results are much more likely to hold in other industrial settings where similar policies are in place. Examining the effect of ownership in contexts where ownership is not stressed as highly, such as in many open source software (OSS) projects, is an area of continued study."

Also from Bird et al.'s framing of *why* the question matters — the cleanest statement of the trade-off in the literature:
> "If ownership has a big effect, then policies to enforce strong code ownership can be put into place… If ownership has little effect, then the normal bottlenecks associated with having one person in charge of each component can be removed, and available talent reassigned at will."

**Google's practice is closer to strong ownership than to collective ownership** — *Software Engineering at Google*, Ch. 9 — https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch09.html
> "Specially named OWNERS files list usernames of people who have ownership responsibilities for a directory and its children."
> "A change might be proposed by any engineer and LGTM'ed by any other engineer, but an owner of the directory in question must also approve this addition to their part of the codebase."
> Ownership "implies a set of responsibilities, such as understanding the code that is owned or knowing how to find somebody who does."

**Practitioner harms of publishing the metric itself** — Jabrayilzade et al., §4.2.5 "Pitfalls of using bus factor," verbatim:
> "The bus factor metric and especially the key engineers part of it may not be received well by the team. Some of the concerns mentioned by the respondents include:
> • Too much attention may be paid to the implicated modules.
> • A key engineer may feel irreplaceable, which may negatively impact their relationship with their employer and teammates (IP1)…
> • Those not listed as key engineers may feel underestimated and uncomfortable about their role in the project.
> • If the bus factor metric is taken at a face value, overestimation of the bus factor may result in false feeling of security.
> • Engineers who work at the projects with low bus factor may be discouraged by the risk or even leave the project."

And their governance recommendation, verbatim:
> "The tool should never be perceived as an ultimate arbiter on the bus factor (or any other health metric) of a project. It should be used as an additional source of information on the project that allows condensing scattered information about the code ownership into a small description with an inevitable loss of context."
> "we believe that the tool should be used on an opt-in basis per team, and the opt-in decision should involve the development team."

Note also from that paper's own framing that the *sign* of the signal is not settled: *"even though a significant share of the open-source projects have experienced bus factor problem, it is unclear whether this result was undesirable or it was simply end of life for a project no longer needed."*

**The 2025–2026 threat to the whole method (AI authorship):**
- Otávio Cury, Guilherme Avelino (the original TF author), "The Impact of Generative AI on Code Expertise Models: An Exploratory Study," arXiv:2507.08160 (2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08160: *"we present an exploratory analysis of how a knowledge model and a Truck Factor algorithm built upon it can be affected by GenAI usage… Our findings reveal that most scenarios led to measurable impacts, indicating the sensitivity of current expertise metrics. This suggests that as GenAI becomes more integrated into development workflows, the reliability of such metrics may decrease."*
- Brett Wheeler, "The Substrate Collapse: AI Code Generation Invalidates Authorship-Based Knowledge Metrics," arXiv:2606.20882 (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20882 — **flagging as a single-author argumentative preprint, not peer-reviewed empirical work**: *"The truck factor, the Degree-of-Authorship metric, and the degree-of-knowledge model all rest on one inference — that authoring a region of code is evidence of understanding it… When an agent generates a module and a human merges it, the version-control record still attributes authorship, but the attribution no longer licenses any conclusion about comprehension: the same footprint is now compatible with full, partial, or no understanding."*

## B1. Tornhill's hotspots: change frequency × complexity

Adam Tornhill, "Software (r)Evolution (Part 1): Predict Maintenance Problems in Large Codebases," CodeScene blog, 9 Aug 2016 — https://codescene.com/blog/software-revolution-part1/

**The power-law premise, verbatim:**
> "The X-axis shows each file in the system sorted on their change frequencies (the number of commits as recorded in the version-control data)… The graphs above show the data from three radically different systems. Systems from different domains, codebases of different size, developed by different organizations and of different age. Yet all graphs show the same power law distribution."
> "The distributions above show that most of our development activity is located in a relatively small part of the total codebase. The majority of all files are in the long tail, which means they represent code that's rarely, if ever, touched."

**Why change frequency alone isn't enough — this is exactly your "not all code is equal" argument, in his words:**
> "the importance of change to a module is so high that more elaborate metrics rarely provide any further predictive value when it comes to fault prediction. However, despite these findings, our model still suffers a weakness. Why, because all code isn't equal. For example, it's a huge difference to increase a simple version number in a single-line file compared to correcting a bug in a file with 5.000 lines of C++ with tricky, nested conditional logic. The first change is low risk and can for all practical purposes be ignored while the second type of change needs extra attention in terms of test and code inspections. Thus, we need to add a second dimension to our model in order to improve its predictive power; We need to add a complexity dimension."

**The definition, verbatim:**
> "A hotspot is complicated code that you have to work with often. Hotspots are calculated from two different data sources: We use the lines of code as a simple proxy for complexity. We calculate the change frequency of each file by mining their version-control history."
> "the number of lines of code is a rough metric, yet it has just as good predictive power as more elaborate metrics like cyclomatic complexity. The advantage of using lines of code lies in the simplicity of the metric; Lines of code is both language neutral and intuitive to reason about."

**The fraction-of-codebase claims — the money quotes, verbatim:**
> "the prioritized Hotspots only make up 2-3% of the total code size. Yet there's a disproportional amount of development activity in that small part with 11-16% of all commits touching those Hotspots. This means any code improvement to a prioritized Hotspot is time well-invested."
> "Our results shows a strong correlation between the top Hotspots and the most defect dense parts in the code. In general, the top Hotspots only make up a minor part of the code, yet that code is responsible for 25-70% of all reported and resolved defects."
> "There's a strong correlation between Hotspots, maintenance costs and software defects."
> "Any improvements we make to the files in the red area… have a high likelihood of providing productivity gains since those files represent code we need to work with all the time."

A concrete worked figure from CodeScene's docs (Hotspots guide, https://docs.enterprise.codescene.io/versions/4.2.2/guides/technical/hotspots.html):
> "The prioritized hotspots only make up 5.5% of the total codebase, yet we spend 17.6% of our development efforts in those hotspots, and 23% of all bugs that we detect and fix are in that small part of the code."
> "Most development activity tends to be located in relatively few modules."

**Tornhill, "Software (r)Evolution (Part 2): Novel Techniques to Prioritize Technical Debt," 25 Aug 2016** — https://codescene.com/blog/software-revolution-part2/ — is the most direct normative statement in this whole thread that code should be weighted, not counted:
> "most code isn't as important as we'd like to think."
> "This finding has important implications because it means that all of your technical debt doesn't matter. You can ignore most of those 4.000 years of potential technical debt and focus on the parts that really matter for your ability to maintain the system."
> "I'm going to go out on a limb here and claim that, by default, we really shouldn't care if some code is badly written or contains excess accidental complexity… Low quality code only matters if we need to work with it, perhaps to fix a bug or extend an existing feature. But of course, then it becomes a true nightmare."
> "The reason that many well-known speakers and authors in the software industry seem obsessed with keeping all code nice and clean is because we cannot know up front in which category code will fall; Is it code that ends up in the long tail that we rarely touch or will we have to modify that piece of code on a regular basis? Hotspots are great because they help us make this divide between the code that matters, the one we need to simplify and improve, and the code whose quality is less important as long as the code does its job."

Use cases he lists for hotspots, verbatim: *"Technical leaders use hotspots for risk management. Making a change to a Hotspot or extending its functionality with new features is high risk. A Hotspot analysis lets you identify those areas up-front so that you can schedule additional time or allocate extra testing efforts. Hotspots point to code review candidates."*

## B2. OpenSSF / Google "Criticality Score" — the actual formula

Repo: https://github.com/ossf/criticality_score · README: https://github.com/ossf/criticality_score/blob/main/README.md
Algorithm paper: **Rob Pike, "Quantifying Criticality"** — https://github.com/ossf/criticality_score/blob/main/Quantifying_criticality_algorithm.pdf (the project was launched by Google's Open Source Security Team; Abhishek Arya, Chris Brown and Rob Pike are the credited authors of the score's write-up). Announcement/explainer: https://openssf.org/blog/2023/07/28/understanding-and-applying-the-openssf-criticality-score-in-open-source-projects/

**Definition, verbatim (README):**
> "A project's criticality score defines the influence and importance of a project. It is a number between 0 (least-critical) and 1 (most-critical)."
> "It is based on the following algorithm by Rob Pike"

**The derivation, verbatim from Pike's paper** (I extracted the full text; this is the actual reasoning chain, which is the useful part):

Naive form:
> "A naive starting point would be to define the criticality value of a package C_pkg as a weighted sum of the signal values for that package: C_pkg = Σ_i α_i S_i"
> "This has several disadvantages. The value is unbounded, which means that the criticality value of a package may grow over time although the true importance of the package is unchanged. Also, many if not most signals are non-linear in effect, with Zipfian-like distributions. A package with 10,000 dependents is surely more important than a package with only 1,000, but arguably not ten times more."

Log-scaled:
> "C_pkg = Σ_i α_i log(1 + S_i)"
> "For one signal, the number of dependents, and a weight of 1, package A with 10,000 dependents has criticality value C_A = 9.2, while package B with 100,000 dependents has C_B = 11.5."

**Final formula, verbatim:**
> "C_pkg = (1 / Σ_i α_i) Σ_i α_i · log(1 + S_i) / log(1 + max(S_i, T_i))"

> "For a signal S_i we choose a threshold value T_i such that any signal value above that is at maximum importance. In other words, we clamp the signal values to a maximum value appropriate to the signal, considering anything above that to be truly 'critical'. For instance, we might consider any package with more than 100,000 dependents to be critical, and ignore the actual count for packages above that threshold."
> "To summarize, for each signal S_i valid within a packaging system we choose two values, a scaling factor α_i representing the relative importance of that signal and a threshold value T_i representing the point at which that signal becomes of maximum importance. For each package, we compute a normalized sum of the ratio of the logarithm of that signal and the logarithm of the maximum of that value and the threshold."

Missing-signal handling, verbatim: *"We can either ignore that signal for that package completely, in which case the other signals that are available rise in importance, or we can set it to zero, in which case its absence reduces the criticality of the package."*

**The default parameter table (`original_pike.yml`), from the README:**

| Parameter | Weight (α) | Max threshold (T) |
|---|---|---|
| created_since | 1 | 120 (months) |
| updated_since | −1 | 120 (months) |
| contributor_count | 2 | 5,000 |
| org_count | 1 | 10 |
| commit_frequency | 1 | 1,000 |
| recent_releases_count | 0.5 | 26 |
| closed_issues_count | 0.5 | 5,000 |
| updated_issues_count | 0.5 | 5,000 |
| comment_frequency | 1 | 15 |
| dependents_count | 2 | 500,000 |

**The two heaviest signals (weight 2) are `dependents_count` and `contributor_count`** — i.e. fan-in and team breadth. Note `updated_since` carries weight −1: staleness reduces criticality. And note this scores *projects*, not files — if you want it at file granularity you'd be re-deriving the shape, not reusing the parameters.

## B3. Churn and defect prediction: the code that changes is the code that breaks

**"Use of Relative Code Churn Measures to Predict System Defect Density,"** Nachiappan Nagappan, Thomas Ball, *ICSE 2005*, pp. 284–292. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/use-of-relative-code-churn-measures-to-predict-system-defect-density/ · PDF: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/icse05churn.pdf · DOI https://doi.org/10.1145/1062455.1062514

**Abstract, verbatim:**
> "We present a technique for early prediction of system defect density using a set of relative code churn measures that relate the amount of churn to other variables such as component size and the temporal extent of churn. Using statistical regression models, we show that while absolute measures of code churn are poor predictors of defect density, our set of relative measures of code churn is highly predictive of defect density. A case study performed on Windows Server 2003 indicates the validity of the relative code churn measures as early indicators of system defect density. Furthermore, our code churn metric suite is able to discriminate between fault and not fault-prone binaries with an accuracy of 89.0 percent."

**Core hypothesis, verbatim:** *"Our basic hypothesis is that code that changes many times pre-release will likely have more post-release defects than code that changes less over the same period of time."*

**The four research hypotheses (Table 1, verbatim):**
> "H1 Increase in relative code churn measures is accompanied by an increase in system defect density"
> "H2 Using relative values of code churn predictors is better than using direct (absolute) values to explain the system defect density"
> "H3 Relative code churn measures can be used as efficient predictors of system defect density."
> "H4 Relative code churn measures can be used to discriminate between fault and not fault-prone binaries."

**The eight measures — I verified these directly against the PDF (a web summarizer got several of these wrong; these are the real ones, Figure 1):**
> M1: Churned LOC / Total LOC
> M2: Deleted LOC / Total LOC
> M3: Files churned / File count
> M4: Churn count / Files churned
> M5: Weeks of churn / File count
> M6: Lines worked on / Weeks of churn
> M7: Churned LOC / Deleted LOC
> M8: Lines worked on / Churn count

Verbatim on M1: *"We expect the larger the proportion of churned (added + changed) code to the LOC of the new binary, the larger the magnitude of the defect density for that binary will be."*
Verbatim result: *"[the relative measures] are better predictors of defect density than the absolute measures. They also they are indicative of increase in system defect density and can accurately predict the system defect density with a high degree of sensitivity. Our metric suite is able to discriminate between fault and not fault-prone binaries in W2k3-SP1 with an accuracy of 89.0 percent."*

**The key architectural insight for your purposes: every one of M1–M8 is a *ratio*. Nagappan & Ball's entire finding is that raw change volume is a poor signal and change volume *normalized by the thing it touches* is a strong one.** That is exactly the blast-radius-weighting argument, established in 2005 on Windows Server 2003.

**"Does Bug Prediction Support Human Developers? Findings From a Google Case Study,"** Chris Lewis, Zhongpeng Lin, Caitlin Sadowski, Xiaoyan Zhu, Rong Ou, E. James Whitehead Jr., *ICSE 2013*. PDF: https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/41145.pdf · https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/2486788.2486838

This is the essential cautionary source — **the metric was right and it still changed nothing.**
> "We deployed a bug prediction algorithm across Google, and found no identifiable change in developer behavior. Using our experience, we provide several characteristics that bug prediction algorithms need to meet in order to be accepted by human developers and truly change how developers evaluate their code."

**The five required characteristics — directly applicable to any risk score you ship:**
> "By far the most desired characteristic is that the output from a bug prediction algorithm is actionable. Once a bug-prone area has been identified, the development team should be able to take clear steps that will result in the area no longer being flagged."
> "Unfortunately, FixCache's reliance on source history means there is nothing that can be done by a team to immediately unflag a file; they must try to improve the health of the file, then wait weeks or months for it to no longer collect bug reports."
> "both will always flag a certain percentage of files, so the code can never be given a clean bill of health. This means that these algorithms never provide developers with any reward, just a revolving door of problems, which is likely very disheartening."
> "Obvious reasoning: When an area is flagged as bug-prone, there must be a strong, visible and obvious reason why the flagging took place, allaying any fear that the flag is a false positive that will only waste developer time. If a developer is convinced that a tool outputs false positives, he or she will ignore it from that point on. The burden of proof is always on the tool to precisely elucidate why it has come to the conclusion it has."
> "Rahman's reasoning is clear and obvious; any developer can quickly believe (and verify) the number of closed bugs on any given file. In contrast, FixCache does not easily offer its reasoning; it is often opaque as to why FixCache has pulled in a file, even with a strong understanding of the algorithm."
> "FixCache's assumption of 10% of files is not feasible for human consumption in almost all cases. In a modest 2000 file project, 200 files will be flagged… Any good bug prediction algorithm for humans must be effective whether it is to flag one file or one hundred."

**Their resulting algorithm, Time-Weighted Risk (TWR), verbatim** — a decay-weighted sum over bug-fixing commits:
> "TWR = Σ_{i=0}^{n} 1 / (1 + e^{−12 t_i + ω})   Where i is a bug-fixing commit, n is the number of bug-fixing commits…"
> "developers were more concerned about files that are currently causing problems… If an algorithm doesn't have actionable messages, it should probably bias itself towards newer issues, rather than taking into account older ones."

The simple, explainable "Rahman" baseline (count of closed bugs per file) beat the sophisticated FixCache in developer judgment: *"The Rahman algorithm performed significantly better than the FixCache algorithms at identifying bug-[prone files]."*

## B4. Core vs. periphery: architectural blast radius

**"The Architecture of Complex Systems: Do Core-Periphery Structures Dominate?"**, Alan MacCormack, Carliss Baldwin, John Rusnak, *Harvard Business School Working Paper 10-059* (2010). PDF: https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/10-059_0cb8fd37-fe3a-49ce-9ed4-5710d0e98342.pdf · SSRN https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.1539115
Companion: MacCormack, Rusnak, Baldwin, **"Exploring the Structure of Complex Software Designs: An Empirical Study of Open Source and Proprietary Code,"** *Management Science* 52(7), 2006 — https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/mnsc.1060.0552 (this is where **propagation cost** is defined: the average proportion of design elements affected when one element is changed; high propagation cost = low modularity).

**Definitions, verbatim:**
> "Definition 1: A complex technological system comprises a number of different subsystems and associated components. Components differ in their degree of centrality. Core components are those that are tightly coupled to other components. Peripheral components are those that are only loosely coupled to other components."
> "Definition 2: Core subsystems are those that contain many core components. Peripheral subsystems are those that contain only a few (or no) core components."

**The operational measure — this is the most directly reusable piece of machinery in Thread B:**
> "By raising the DSM to successive powers of n, we obtain the direct and indirect dependencies that exist for successive path lengths n. Summing these matrices yields the visibility matrix… Fan-In Visibility (FIV) is obtained by summing down the columns; Fan-Out Visibility (FOV) is obtained by summing along the rows."
> "We define a 'Core' component as one that is tightly coupled to many other components in both directions. That is, many other components depend upon it (i.e., it has a high FIV) and it depends upon many other components (i.e., it has a high FOV). To evaluate whether a component meets this criterion, we observe the maximum level of visibility for each measure, and define those that exceed 50% of this value as 'high.'"

**The four canonical types, verbatim from Table 1:**
> "Core Components: High FIV, High FOV — Files with high visibility on both measures are 'Core' files. They are 'seen by' many files and 'see' many files."
> "Shared Components: High FIV, Low FOV — Files with high FIV are 'Shared' files. They provide shared functionality to many different parts of the system."
> "Peripheral Components: Low FIV, Low FOV — Files with low visibility on both measures are 'Peripheral' files… They typically execute independently of other files."
> "Control Components: Low FIV, High FOV — Files with high VFO are 'Control' files. They direct the flow of program control to different parts of the system."

**Empirical findings, verbatim:**
> "We find that 1027 of the 1286 releases (80%) possess a core-periphery structure… Focusing only on the distinct applications in our sample, we find that 14 of the 19 systems tend to exhibit a core-periphery structure (74%). We conclude that core-periphery structures dominate this sample. However, the fact that there are exceptions to this pattern is important. Software systems do not have to possess such a structure."
> "The size of the core for the six resulting systems varies between 38 and 209 components. On a proportionate basis, this represents from 12% to 64% of a system."
> Core-as-%-of-system for comparably sized systems: MyBooks 64.30%, PostgreSQL 62.2%, Berkeley DB 45.9%, Gnumeric 45.3%.

**The critical methodological warning — you cannot eyeball this, you must compute transitive closure:**
> "We found no variable that could reliably predict whether a system possessed a Core-periphery structure, and no consistent pattern of dependencies in the Design Structure Matrix that would signal the presence of such a structure… Analysis reveals that the system on the left has no core, while the one on the right has a large core comprising 37% of the system. This indicates the role played by indirect dependencies… We conclude that detecting the presence of a Core-periphery structure cannot be achieved solely by examining the direct dependencies for a system, but requires an assessment of all potential paths through which dependencies propagate."

Also from the 2010 paper's abstract framing: *"Open, distributed organizations tend to develop systems with smaller cores"* — i.e. the org shape and the blast-radius shape are coupled (the mirroring hypothesis, tested in MacCormack, Rusnak & Baldwin, "Exploring the Duality Between Product and Organizational Architectures," HBS WP 08-039, https://www.hbs.edu/ris/download.aspx?name=08-038.pdf).

## B5. Criticality tiering in production: Google SRE

*Site Reliability Engineering* (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, eds., O'Reilly 2016), Ch. 21 "Handling Overload" — https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/

**Google's four-value criticality enum, verbatim:**
> "CRITICAL_PLUS — Reserved for the most critical requests, those that will result in serious user-visible impact if they fail."
> "CRITICAL — The default value for requests sent from production jobs. These requests will result in user-visible impact, but the impact may be less severe than those of CRITICAL_PLUS."
> "SHEDDABLE_PLUS — Traffic for which partial unavailability is expected. This is the default for batch jobs, which can retry requests minutes or even hours later."
> "SHEDDABLE — Traffic for which frequent partial unavailability and occasional full unavailability is expected."

> "we significantly extended our RPC system to propagate criticality automatically" — downstream requests inherit the caller's criticality by default, so load-shedding decisions are consistent across the whole call stack.

The structural lesson for a blast-radius weight: **Google made criticality a first-class, inherited, propagated attribute of a request rather than a per-service configuration lookup.** The equivalent for code would be a criticality attribute that propagates along the dependency graph, not one assigned file-by-file.

Ch. 3 "Embracing Risk" — https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/ — for error budgets: an error budget is 1 − SLO; *"The main benefit of an error budget is that it provides a common incentive that allows both product development and SRE to focus on finding the right balance between innovation and reliability."* SLO targets are set per criticality tier, and a rule of thumb is that a service's critical dependencies need one extra nine relative to the service itself.

## B6. Ownership-based criticality in practice

CODEOWNERS/OWNERS is the most widely deployed real-world criticality-tiering mechanism, and it encodes it as *who must approve*, not as a score — *Software Engineering at Google*, Ch. 9 (https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch09.html): OWNERS files *"act as a kind of documentation, making it easy for people and tools to find those responsible for a given piece of code"*, and *"an owner of the directory in question must also approve this addition to their part of the codebase."*

CodeScene's commercial framing of the same idea (https://codescene.com/resources/use-cases/technical-debt-management):
> "Static code analysis is not enough to prioritize. They just flags 'bad code'. But without historical context, you don't know high-impact areas."
> "Pinpoint the most complex and frequently changed areas of your codebase and prioritize refactoring efforts effectively."

# Synthesis: where the two threads actually join

Three defensible, sourced positions:

1. **Concentration alone is not a defect — concentration × criticality is.** This is Tornhill's own operationalization: a knowledge island in healthy, rarely-touched code is *lower* risk to onboard than a hotspot; the risk case is *"A module that's written mostly by one developer, and that module is a hotspot with code health issues"* (CodeScene docs). And it is what JetBrains' interviewees asked for unprompted: *"Information on criticality of the implicated parts (IP7, IP9)"* and *"IP1 and survey respondents has also mentioned they would like to be able to set manually the importance weights for the files"* (Jabrayilzade et al., ICSE-SEIP 2022). **The bus factor literature knows its file-weighting is missing and has said so out loud.**

2. **The pro-concentration evidence is real and comes from the same lab as the pro-spreading evidence.** Bird, Nagappan et al. (FSE 2011) find, on Windows Vista and 7, that *"high levels of ownership… are associated with less defects"* and that *"the number of minor contributors has a strong positive relationship with both pre- and post-release failures."* Anyone treating "one dominant author" as an unconditional negative signal has to answer this paper. The honest framing: high top-owner ownership is good for **defect risk**; it is bad for **continuity risk**. They are different risks with opposite signs, and the bus factor literature only measures the second.

3. **Nagappan & Ball already proved the normalization principle.** Absolute churn is a poor predictor; churn *relative to what it touches* discriminates fault-prone binaries at 89.0% accuracy. The direct analogue: a raw count of commits or lines is a weak signal, and the same volume normalized by the criticality/size/fan-in of the code touched is a strong one. And Pike's criticality formula supplies the shape for combining heterogeneous signals into one bounded [0,1] number without drift: log-scale each signal, clamp at a per-signal threshold, weight, normalize by Σα.

## Gaps and caveats worth flagging

- **The Cosentino SANER 2015 PDF is paywalled** and every mirror I tried (ResearchGate, Academia.edu, HAL/Inria, CiteSeerX) returned 403 or an access-denied page. Its definition and algorithm above are quoted through two secondary sources that quote it directly; I could not verify against the original.
- The **"25–70% of all reported and resolved defects"** hotspot claim is CodeScene's own internal validation, not peer-reviewed — Tornhill states it as *"Our results shows…"* on the company blog. The peer-reviewable version is the concrete 5.5% / 17.6% / 23% example in the docs.
- **The DOA coefficients (3.293 / 1.098 / 0.164 / −0.321) are fitted to 246 self-ratings from seven developers on one project in 2010** (R² = 0.25). Every subsequent truck-factor paper reuses them unchanged. That is the weakest joint in the whole method, and JetBrains threw them out and refit (`3·FA`, `½ DL`, `2.4 log`, `1.2 log`) for their own multimodal version.
- **No decay term.** Avelino's DOA has no time weighting, which is why Jabrayilzade et al. caught it naming key developers whose last commit was 1.5 years old. Practitioner intuition on the right decay: median knowledge half-life of **4 months**.
- Avelino's **50% file-abandonment threshold contradicts practitioner intuition** — surveyed engineers mostly said "less than 20% of the files can be abandoned before project gets into trouble."
